newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX crude, products slip amid supply overhang.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX crude, products slip amid supply overhang.

text.p: NYMEX crude oil and products prices slid Monday as worries about unrest in Nigeria and a possible strike in California were outweighed by a supply overhang, particularly from the North Sea.
May crude futures fell 45 cents to settle at $21.06 a barrel, just off the day's low of $21.02. April gasoline fell 1.13 cents to 66.51 cents a gallon.
Traders said that both the crude and gasoline futures were being hit by reversal of speculative positions and selling by refiners looking to lock in fairly attractive gasoline-to-crude spreads.

"A lot of the speculative funds have been buying gasoline and selling crude and the refiners are the natural sell-hedge into something like that," said Gerry Samuels, a trader at ARB Oil in California.
"With the strength of gasoline cracks a lot of refiners have been looking at what happened last year after Memorial Day when the gas started sliding off," he added.

Gasoline "crack-spreads" - front-month gasoline versus crude - have been stronger in the past month than they were at this time last year when they ended up soaring to about $10 on worries about low stocks.
The crack has recently been between $6 and $7, about $1 above the range this time last year.

"Gasoline has confirmed that the seasonal really is well under way," says Tim Evans of Pegasus Econometric Group. "The year-on-year inventory shortfall and rising open interest both support the advance."
But despite gasoline's relative strength, it has been slipping since late last week, partly due to refiner selling of cracks at attractive levels.
Also contributing to Monday's loss was the negotiations between workers at Unocal's three California refineries and management at Tosco, which will take the plants over in April.
Workers had threatened to strike on Monday after rejecting a company offer last week.

The unrest in Nigeria, where protesting villagers took hostage workers at one of the main Nigerian oilfields run by Royal Dutch/Shell Group, will disrupt production but not contracted exports, Shell said.
Traders focused instead on the supply overhang from the North Sea where a number of cargoes of benchmark Brent Blend were seen without buyers.
